title: Metadata, Images, Fonts, and Scripts
summary: Give every page its title and preview, serve right-sized images with next/image, load fonts without layout shift, and add third-party scripts safely.
intro: A shop can work perfectly and still lose visitors before they arrive: a search result titled Create Next App, a shared link with no picture, a product photo that takes four seconds on a phone, text that jumps when the font loads, a chat widget that makes every tap feel slow. These are the last things you fix before shipping, and Next.js has a tool for each. This lesson covers the tags that name and describe each page, the files that give your site its icons, share images, and sitemap, images resized and converted for every screen, fonts served from your own site with no jump, third-party scripts that wait their turn, and where your CSS goes, including a dark theme that never flashes.

steps.title: Titles, descriptions, and link previews
steps.body:
Before anyone opens your page, they meet its metadata: the title and description in a search result, and the picture and words in a link preview when someone shares it in a chat. You met these tags in the web course, written by hand in the `head`. A React app that sets them from JavaScript, as the React course did, leaves them out of the HTML until the scripts run, and many of the programs that read them never run scripts. Next.js writes them into the HTML on the server, from an object you export.

## The metadata object

Export a `metadata` object from a layout or a page, and Next.js turns it into tags in the `head`:

```tsx sketch
import type { Metadata } from "next";

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: "Trailhead",
  description: "Packs, tents, and camp gear for long days outside.",
};
```

Only Server Components can export it, since it's read on the server. Every route gets two tags you don't write: `<meta charset="utf-8">` and the viewport tag, which the web course explained.

## A title template

Every page should have its own title, ending with the site's name. Rather than typing `| Trailhead` on every page, set a **template** in the root layout:

```tsx sketch
title: {
  template: "%s | Trailhead",
  default: "Trailhead",
},
```

The template applies to the pages and layouts below this one: a page whose title is `Trail Pack 45L` gets `<title>Trail Pack 45L | Trailhead</title>`, with `%s` replaced. `default` is the title for a page that sets none, like the home page, and it's required whenever you set a template.

## Metadata from data: generateMetadata

A product page's title is the product's name, which comes from the API. For that, export an async function, `generateMetadata`, which you met in the lesson on fetching data, instead of the object. It receives the same `params` as the page, a promise you await, and returns the same shape. The first example uses it.

It calls `getProduct`, the cached data function from the caching lesson, which the page calls too. Because the result is cached, the API is asked once, not twice. And since the product pages are prerendered with `generateStaticParams`, their tags are worked out at build time and sit in the static HTML.

## Absolute addresses: metadataBase

Some tags need a full address, with `https://` and the host: the canonical link, and the URL and image of a link preview. Set `metadataBase` once in the root layout, like `new URL("https://trailhead.example")`, and write those fields as paths. Next.js joins the two. A relative path with no `metadataBase` stops the build.

## Canonical, robots, and Open Graph

A few more fields do most of the work:

- `alternates.canonical` names the one address search engines should list for a page. The same product can be reached as `/products/trail-pack-45?ref=email` and a dozen other ways, and the canonical link says they're all one page.
- `robots` tells search engines whether to list a page and follow its links. `robots: { index: false }` keeps a page like the cart out of results. When a page calls `notFound()` after its HTML has started streaming, the status has already gone out as 200, so Next.js adds `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` itself to keep the missing page out of search.
- `openGraph` fills the **Open Graph** tags from the web course, which chat apps and social sites read to build a link preview: `og:title`, `og:url`, `og:image`, and more. Next.js also writes matching `twitter:` tags, which some sites read instead.

## Merging is shallow

Each layout and page on the way to a route adds its metadata, and the page closest to the URL wins. That merge is **shallow**: a page that sets `openGraph` replaces the layout's whole `openGraph` object, not just the keys it names. Set `siteName` in the layout and `title` in the page, and the page loses `siteName`. The fix in the example is a small shared object, spread into both.

Theme colors and the viewport tag have their own export, `viewport`, next to `metadata`.

examples.title: A title template and a product's metadata
examples.prompt: The shared Open Graph fields, the root layout's metadata, and the product page's `generateMetadata`, from three files.
examples.explanation: Three files work together. `shared-metadata.ts` holds the Open Graph fields every page shares. The root layout sets the base address, the title template with its default, the site's description, and the shared Open Graph fields. The product page's `generateMetadata` awaits `params`, fetches the product, and sends a missing one to the 404 page with `notFound()`. It returns the product's name as the title, which the template completes, its description, a canonical path, and Open Graph fields that spread the shared ones first, so `siteName` and `type` survive the shallow merge. Both paths are relative, and `metadataBase` turns them into full addresses.

examples.title: The tags in the product page's HTML
examples.prompt: With the app built and running (`npm run build`, then `npm run start`), pick the title, meta, and canonical tags out of a product page. Mac and Linux only.

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"/>
<meta name="next-size-adjust" content=""/>
<title>Trail Pack 45L | Trailhead</title>
<meta name="description" content="A 45-liter pack for multi-day trips, with a floating lid, an adjustable torso, and side pockets you can reach while walking."/>
<link rel="canonical" href="https://trailhead.example/products/trail-pack-45"/>

<meta property="og:description" content="A 45-liter pack for multi-day trips, with a floating lid, an adjustable torso, and side pockets you can reach while walking."/>
<meta property="og:url" content="https://trailhead.example/products/trail-pack-45"/>

examples.explanation: These are the tags Next.js wrote into the product page's HTML, picked out with `grep`. The title is the product's name finished by the template. The description and `og:description` both come from the one `description` field, since Next.js copies it into Open Graph when you don't set one there. The canonical link and `og:url` are full addresses, joined from `metadataBase` and the paths. `og:site_name` and `og:type` are here because the page spread the shared object. The `twitter:` tags were added from the same values, and `next-size-adjust` comes from the font setup in part 4. A preview bot reading this page needs no JavaScript at all.

steps.title: Icons, share images, sitemaps, and robots
steps.body:
Some metadata isn't a tag but a file: the little icon on a browser tab, the icon a phone puts on its home screen, the picture in a link preview, and two files search engines look for at fixed addresses, `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml`. In Next.js you make each one by giving a file the right name in `app/`. Next.js serves it and adds the tags that point to it.

## Icons

- `favicon.ico` in the root of `app/` is the tab icon. create-next-app gives you one.
- `icon.png` (or `.jpg`, `.svg`, `.ico`) is a sharper icon, and can sit in any route folder to give that part of the site its own.
- `apple-icon.png` is the icon a phone uses when someone adds your site to the home screen, usually 180 by 180 pixels.

Next.js reads each file's size and type, and writes the tags for you, like `<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-icon.png?apple-icon.3j8m8m2c2j56a.png" sizes="180x180" type="image/png">`. The code after `?` changes whenever the file does, so browsers that cached the old icon fetch the new one.

## A share image for every product

A link preview with a picture gets far more clicks than one without. An `opengraph-image.png` in a route folder becomes that route's `og:image`. For a picture per product, make the file `opengraph-image.tsx` and draw it with code.

The file exports a function that returns an `ImageResponse` from `next/og`. You describe the image in JSX with inline styles, and Next.js turns it into a PNG. It supports flexbox and a subset of CSS, not grid. One rule trips everyone: a `div` with more than one child needs `display: "flex"`. Without it, the image fails, and the server log says `Expected <div> to have explicit "display: flex", "display: contents", or "display: none" if it has more than one child node.` Next to the function, three exports describe the image: `alt`, `size`, and `contentType`, which become the `og:image:alt`, width, height, and type tags. The first example draws one.

Generated images are made at build time when they can be. This one awaits `params`, so on its own it would run on every request. Exporting `generateStaticParams` from the image file, with the same slugs as the page, lets the build make one PNG per product. The route table marks them ●, prerendered for each value of the dynamic segment.

## robots.txt

A **crawler** is the program a search engine sends to read pages, following link after link. `robots.txt` is a plain text file at the root of a site that tells crawlers which paths to skip. It's a request, not a lock: polite crawlers obey it, and anyone can still visit the paths. Write `app/robots.ts`, return an object, and Next.js serves the text at `/robots.txt`.

## sitemap.xml

A **sitemap** lists the pages you want found, in an XML format search engines agree on. A shop with thousands of products shouldn't hope crawlers stumble on each one. `app/sitemap.ts` returns an array with one entry per page, built from your data, and Next.js serves it as XML at `/sitemap.xml`. Since it calls the cached `listProducts`, it's prerendered too, and it's made again when the product list's cache runs out.

## manifest

`app/manifest.ts` returns a **web app manifest**, the file that tells a phone how to install your site like an app: its name, colors, and icons. Next.js serves it at `/manifest.webmanifest` and adds `<link rel="manifest">` to every page.

All of these are special Route Handlers, the kind of route from the Route Handlers lesson, and they're cached like pages unless they read request data such as cookies.

examples.title: A share image drawn for each product
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/opengraph-image.tsx`, which draws a 1200 by 630 preview picture for every product at build time.
examples.explanation: 1200 by 630 pixels is the size most preview cards expect. The outer `div` fills the image and stacks three lines with flexbox: the shop's name, the product's name, and its price. The price is built as one string first, since writing `$` and then `{...}` next to each other would make two children, and a `div` with two children needs `display: "flex"`. With this file in the folder, the product page's HTML gains `og:image` with an address like `https://trailhead.example/products/trail-pack-45/opengraph-image?1231a08b49317d1a`, plus its alt text, width, height, type, and the matching `twitter:image` tags. Fetched, that address answers `content-type: image/png` with the 1200 by 630 picture.

Each entry became a `url` element with its full address in `loc`. `head -12` keeps the first 12 lines, and the file goes on with the other 11 products. The `head` command is on Mac and Linux.

steps.title: Images with next/image
steps.body:
Images are usually the heaviest thing on a page, and the biggest one is often the **Largest Contentful Paint**, the LCP from the web course: the moment the main content shows up. The web course showed how to do images well by hand: `width` and `height` so nothing jumps, `srcset` and `sizes` so a phone downloads a small file, modern formats like WebP and AVIF, and `loading="lazy"` for images further down. `next/image` does all of that from one component, and makes the smaller files for you.

## What you write

The product page shows its photo like this:

```tsx sketch
<Image
  src={product.imageUrl}
  alt={product.name}
  width={1200}
  height={800}
  sizes="(min-width: 768px) 50vw, 100vw"
  preload
/>
```

`src` is the product's `imageUrl` from the API, a path in `public/` like `/images/products/trail-pack-45.webp`. `width` and `height` give the shape, so the browser saves the right space before the file arrives. `sizes` says how wide the image is drawn: half the window on screens 768 pixels wide or more, the whole window below that. `preload` is for the LCP image, explained below.

## What it renders

The first example shows the HTML. The `srcSet` lists nine versions, from 384 to 3840 pixels wide, and every one points at `/_next/image`, Next.js's **image optimizer**, with the source path, a width `w`, and a quality `q` of 75. The browser reads `sizes`, works out how many pixels it needs on this screen, and asks for the closest width. In a 1280-pixel-wide window on an ordinary screen, half is 640, so it asked for `w=640`.

```diagram metadata-images-fonts-image-fan
One source photo becomes many widths and formats, each made when first asked for.
```

## The optimizer

The first time anyone asks for a version, the server makes it: it reads the source, resizes it with **sharp**, an image library that's installed with Next.js, and encodes it in the best format the browser's `Accept` header allows. Then it saves the result in `.next/cache/images` and serves the copy from then on. By default that format is WebP, and a browser that doesn't list WebP gets a JPEG, even when the source file is itself a WebP. AVIF files are smaller still but slower to make, so they're opt-in: `images: { formats: ["image/avif", "image/webp"] }` in `next.config.ts`.

The optimizer only makes what you allowed, since otherwise anyone could make your server resize images all day:

- Widths come from two lists in `next.config.ts`, `deviceSizes` and `imageSizes`, with sensible defaults. Any other width is refused.
- Qualities must be in `images.qualities`, which is `[75]` unless you add more. Next.js 16 made this list required.
- Remote images, from another host, need a matching entry in `remotePatterns`. List the exact host and path, like `{ protocol: "https", hostname: "cdn.trailhead.example", pathname: "/products/**" }`.
- `localPatterns` limits which paths in your own site can be optimized.

The second example shows the optimizer's answers, the refusals included.

## Images that fill a box

When the box's size comes from CSS, like a product card that's always 3 by 2, use `fill` instead of `width` and `height`. The image stretches over its parent, which needs `position: relative`, and `className="object-cover"` crops it to fit. Always pair `fill` with `sizes`. Without it, Next.js assumes the image is as wide as the window and offers only big files.

## The LCP image: preload

Every image is lazy by default: it gets `loading="lazy"`, so the browser waits until it's near the screen. That's wrong for the one big image at the top, which should start loading at once. In Next.js 16, the `preload` prop does that: it puts a `<link rel="preload" as="image">` with the same `srcset` in the `head`, so the browser starts the download before it even reaches the `img`. It replaced the older `priority` prop, which still works but is deprecated. Use `preload` on one image per page, the one you know is the LCP. When different images could be the biggest depending on the screen, the docs suggest `loading="eager"` or `fetchPriority="high"` on them instead.

Images you import, like `import photo from "./trail.jpg"`, get their width and height read at build time, and a name with a content hash, so they can be cached forever.

examples.title: The img tag next/image rendered
examples.prompt: With the app running, pull the product photo's `img` tag out of the page, one attribute per line.
examples.explanation: The `sed` puts most attributes on a line of their own, on Mac and Linux. `width` and `height` are here, so the space is saved before the photo loads. There's no `loading="lazy"`, because `preload` marks this as the image to load first. `sizes` is passed through as you wrote it. `srcSet` is the list the browser chooses from: nine widths, each an `/_next/image` address with the source path percent-encoded, `%2F` being a slash, and `&` the character reference for `&`. `src` is the fallback for browsers that ignore `srcset`. A card on the home page with `fill` gets `loading="lazy"` instead, and a `style` of `position:absolute;height:100%;width:100%` that stretches it over its box.

examples.title: What the image optimizer answers
examples.prompt: Ask `/_next/image` for the 640-pixel version the way a browser does, then try a quality, a width, and a host that aren't allowed.
examples.code:
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - -H "Accept: image/avif,image/webp,*/*" "http://127.0.0.1:3005/_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fproducts%2Ftrail-pack-45.webp&w=640&q=75"
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:3005/_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fproducts%2Ftrail-pack-45.webp&w=640&q=80"; echo
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:3005/_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fproducts%2Ftrail-pack-45.webp&w=650&q=75"; echo
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:3005/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fcat.jpg&w=640&q=75"; echo
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Vary: Accept
Cache-Control: public, max-age=14400, must-revalidate
ETag: XGKR0wVLcoacfrq5yF9bMheh9XLOUQ6nr30vAr_mpqE
Content-Type: image/webp
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="trail-pack-45.webp"
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'none'; frame-src 'none'; sandbox;
X-Nextjs-Cache: MISS
Content-Length: 2730
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:08:56 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

"q" parameter (quality) of 80 is not allowed
"w" parameter (width) of 650 is not allowed
"url" parameter is not allowed
examples.explanation: The first request asks like a browser does, with an `Accept` header listing AVIF and WebP. The answer is `image/webp`, since AVIF isn't turned on, and `Vary: Accept` tells caches that the answer depends on that header. `X-Nextjs-Cache: MISS` means this version was made just now, and asking again says `HIT`. `Cache-Control` lets browsers keep it for 14,400 seconds, four hours, the default `minimumCacheTTL`. The source here is a simple test graphic, a 2400 by 1600 WebP of 20,548 bytes, so 2,730 bytes is far smaller than a real photo would get, but the saving is real. Asked without WebP in `Accept`, the same address answers `image/jpeg`, 5,085 bytes. Then come three refusals with status 400: a quality not in `qualities`, a width not in the lists, and a host not in `remotePatterns`.

examples.explanation: The first command prints the home page's `Link` header. It names two font files to preload, the Latin files of Geist and Geist Mono, both on this site's own `/_next/static/media` path, never on a font service. A `Link` header with `rel=preload` works like a `<link rel="preload">` tag, and arriving with the headers, it starts the download before the browser has read any HTML. examples.title: The fallback face in the built CSS
examples.prompt: In the project folder, after a build, find the font rules Next.js and Tailwind generated.
examples.explanation: Run in the project folder after `npm run build`, this picks three kinds of rule out of the built CSS. The first is the fallback face: `local(Arial)` means use the Arial already on the computer, and the four overrides reshape it to Geist's measurements, making it 104.76% of its normal size with matching space above and below each line. The next two are the `variable` classes on `html`, each defining a font variable that lists the real font first and its fallback second. The last is Tailwind's `font-sans` utility, made from `@theme`, which reads that variable. The class names come from a hash, so yours will differ.

steps.title: Third-party scripts
steps.body:
Most sites carry code they didn't write: analytics, a chat bubble, a reviews widget, a map, a video player. Each one is JavaScript from someone else's server that runs on the same **main thread** as your page, the single thread that also handles taps and clicks. A heavy one makes the page slow to respond, which hurts **INP**, Interaction to Next Paint, the web course's measure of how fast a page reacts. One loaded early fights your LCP image for bandwidth. A plain `<script>` tag in the `head` even stops the browser reading the page until it has run. `next/script` lets you say when each one should load.

## The Script component and its strategies

```tsx sketch
import Script from "next/script";

<Script src="/reviews-widget.js" strategy="lazyOnload" />
```

`strategy` picks the moment:

| Strategy | When it loads | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| `afterInteractive` | early, once some of the page has hydrated | the default, for analytics and tag managers |
| `lazyOnload` | when the browser is idle, after everything else has loaded | chat bubbles, review widgets, anything below the fold |
| `beforeInteractive` | before Next.js's own code, from the server's HTML | rare must-run-first code, like a cookie consent manager |
| `worker` | in a web worker, off the main thread | experimental, and it doesn't work with the App Router yet |

Hydration, recall, is React attaching its handlers to the server's HTML, and it's the point where the page starts to react. `afterInteractive` waits for some of it, so your own code goes first. `lazyOnload` waits for the page's load event and a quiet moment. Tried on the product page, the widget's request came after the load event, and its `script` tag was added at the end of `body`. A `beforeInteractive` script must sit in the root layout. It's always placed in the `head`, and fetched before any of Next.js's code, though it doesn't hold up hydration. Use it only when the script truly has to run first.

Wherever you put a `Script`, Next.js loads it once. Navigating between pages that both include it doesn't load it again. Put a script in the layout of the routes that need it, not in the root layout, so pages that don't use it don't pay for it.

## Running code when it loads

Many widgets need a call after they load, like `Widget.init()`. `onLoad` runs once the script has loaded, `onReady` runs then and again each time the component mounts, and `onError` runs if it fails. They're functions, so they only work in a Client Component. `onLoad` can't be used with `beforeInteractive`, and `onReady` can.

A script written inline, between the tags instead of in a file, needs an `id`, so Next.js can tell it's the same script on every render.

## Ready-made embeds: @next/third-parties

The `@next/third-parties` package wraps a few common Google services in components that load the right way: `GoogleTagManager`, `GoogleAnalytics`, `GoogleMapsEmbed`, and `YouTubeEmbed`, plus `sendGTMEvent` and `sendGAEvent` for sending events. `YouTubeEmbed` uses a **facade**: it shows a light stand-in with the video's thumbnail and loads the real player only when someone presses play. The package is marked experimental, so pin its version to the one that matches your `next`.

## Count what each one costs

Every tag someone asks you to add has a price in bytes and main-thread time, paid by every visitor. Before adding one, ask whether it can wait until idle, whether a facade would do, and whether it's needed on every page. Then check with Lighthouse or the Performance panel from the web course, before and after. A strict Content Security Policy, from the lesson on secrets and security, also has to allow each script, which is one more reason to keep the list short.

examples.title: A widget that loads when the page is idle
examples.prompt: A Client Component that loads a reviews widget's script with `lazyOnload` and mounts it with `onReady`.
examples.explanation: A third-party reviews widget, made up for this example, wrapped in its own Client Component, `app/products/[slug]/reviews-widget.tsx`, because `onReady` is a function. The empty `div` is where the widget draws itself, with the product named in a `data-` attribute. `lazyOnload` keeps the script out of the way until the page has loaded and the browser is idle. `onReady` mounts the widget after the script loads, and again if the visitor leaves the page and comes back, when the script is already loaded and `onLoad` wouldn't fire. The `?.` skips the call if the script defined nothing. In TypeScript, you'd also declare `ExampleReviews` on `window`.

examples.title: Google Analytics with @next/third-parties
examples.prompt: The root layout with Google's analytics tag added through the `GoogleAnalytics` component.
examples.explanation: `app/layout.tsx` with Google Analytics added through `@next/third-parties`, which you install with `npm install @next/third-parties` at the same version as `next`. `G-XYZ` stands for your measurement ID from Google. The component loads Google's tag script after hydration, the same timing as `afterInteractive`, and sets up its data layer, so you don't paste Google's snippet by hand. Placed in the root layout, it loads on every page. To send an event from a button, a Client Component calls `sendGAEvent`.

steps.title: Styling, global CSS, and themes
steps.body:
CSS in a Next.js app goes in three places: Tailwind classes in your components, a little global CSS, and the occasional CSS Module. Knowing where each belongs keeps styles from fighting, and it's also where the last bug of this lesson hides: a dark theme that flashes white on every load. ## Tailwind, as create-next-app sets it up You met Tailwind in the web course. In a Next.js 16.4 project made with create-next-app, three pieces wire it up, as the lesson that created the project showed: - `app/globals.css` starts with `@import "tailwindcss";`, and holds the `@theme` block from part 4. - `app/layout.tsx` imports that file once, with `import "./globals.css";`. - `next.config.ts` runs Tailwind on CSS files with a **loader**, a step that transforms a file before the bundler uses it. The starter adds `@tailwindcss/turbopack` under `turbopack.rules`, since Turbopack is the bundler Next.js 16 uses. The Next.js docs, and many older projects, wire it through PostCSS instead, with `@tailwindcss/postcss` in a `postcss.config.mjs`. Both run the same Tailwind 4, and your classes work the same either way. ## One catch: CSS Modules The starter's rule matches every file ending in `.css`, and that includes CSS Modules. A **CSS Module** is a file named like `product.module.css` whose class names are made unique per file, so `.price` in one module never clashes with `.price` in another. You import it as an object, `import styles from "./product.module.css"`, and write `className={styles.price}`. With the starter's rule, a module comes out as plain global CSS: `styles.price` is `undefined`, and the built page had `

` with no class at all. Telling the rule to skip modules fixes it, as the first example shows. After that change, the same `

` came out as `

`, with a matching `.aEjafq_price` rule in the built CSS. ## Where global CSS goes Import global CSS, like `globals.css`, in the root layout. Any layout or page can import a CSS file, but Next.js doesn't remove a stylesheet when you navigate away from the page that loaded it, so global rules imported deep in the app leak onto other pages. Keep global CSS for what's truly global: Tailwind itself, your theme's custom properties, and base styles for `body`. Styles come out in the order you import them, so keep those imports at the top of the root layout. ## Dark mode without a flash Following the system's setting is easy: the starter's `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` rule is pure CSS, so the browser picks the right colors before it paints anything. A theme the visitor chooses is harder. Their choice lives in a cookie or in `localStorage`, and the server's HTML doesn't know it. Reading the cookie with `cookies()` in the root layout would make every page in the app dynamic, giving up the static shells from the caching lessons. Setting the theme in a `useEffect` runs after the first paint, so dark-mode visitors see a white flash on every load. The fix the Next.js docs give is a tiny **inline script**, written straight into the HTML in the `head`. The browser runs it while reading the page, before it paints anything. It reads the cookie and sets `data-theme` on `html`. Three details make it work: - `suppressHydrationWarning` on `html`, since the script changes an attribute before React hydrates, and React would otherwise report a mismatch between the server's HTML and the page. - A `try` around it, because cookies and storage can be blocked. - A Tailwind variant that follows the attribute instead of the system, so `dark:bg-black` means when `data-theme` is `dark`: `@custom-variant dark (&:where([data-theme="dark"], [data-theme="dark"] *));`. To switch themes, a button sets the attribute and writes the cookie: `document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark")`, then `document.cookie = "theme=dark; path=/; max-age=31536000; SameSite=Lax"`. Tried in a browser with a `theme=dark` cookie, the page came up with `data-theme="dark"` and the dark background. A strict Content Security Policy blocks inline scripts unless they carry a nonce, as the lesson on secrets and security showed.

examples.title: Keeping CSS Modules out of the Tailwind rule
examples.prompt: `next.config.ts` as create-next-app made it, with one `condition` line added so CSS Modules work.
examples.explanation: This is the starter's `next.config.ts` with one line added. `cacheComponents` and `partialPrefetching` are the caching and prefetching settings from earlier lessons. Under `turbopack.rules`, the key `"*.css"` matches every CSS file, `loaders` runs Tailwind's loader on it, and `as` says the result is still CSS. The added `condition` makes the rule skip any path ending in `.module.css`, so modules go through Next.js's own CSS Modules handling and keep their unique class names. Modules then skip Tailwind's processing, which suits them: Tailwind classes belong in `className`, and modules hold the styles Tailwind doesn't cover.

examples.title: A theme script that runs before paint
examples.prompt: The root layout with an inline script in the `head` that applies a saved theme before the page is drawn.
examples.explanation: The root layout in `app/layout.tsx`, with the imports, fonts, and metadata from earlier parts left out. `html` starts as `data-theme="light"`, the theme for anyone without a cookie. The script is a string, wrapped in a function that runs at once, and `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` writes it into the HTML as it is, since React won't run a script given as children. It finds a `theme` cookie, and if there is one, copies its value onto `html`. In `globals.css`, a `[data-theme="dark"]` rule changes the `--background` and `--foreground` custom properties, so the whole page follows. The page stays fully static, since the server never reads the cookie. `body` also gets `font-sans`, the fix from part 4. With every page named, sized, and styled, the next lesson builds the shop for production and puts it online.

recap:
- Export metadata or generateMetadata from layouts and pages, with a title template and metadataBase in the root layout.
- Metadata merges shallowly, so share nested objects like openGraph by spreading a common one.
- Name files to make metadata: favicon and apple-icon, opengraph-image.tsx with ImageResponse, robots.ts, sitemap.ts, and manifest.ts.
- next/image writes width, height, srcset, and lazy loading, and its optimizer makes each width in WebP from an allowlist of sizes and qualities.
- Mark the one LCP image with preload, which replaced priority in Next.js 16, and pair fill with sizes.
- next/font downloads fonts at build, serves them from your own site, and adds a size-matched fallback so text doesn't jump.
- Load third-party code with next/script and the latest strategy that works, usually afterInteractive or lazyOnload.
- Import global CSS in the root layout, keep the Tailwind loader off CSS Modules, and set a saved theme with an inline script in the head.
